Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡({{field-1}})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡({{field-2}}).
$$

The constant coefficient of the series is

$$
{a}_{0}={{field-3}}.
$$

Given that $F(x)={cos}^{2}⁡(x)$ and $L=4,$ the constant coefficient becomes

$$
{a}_{0}={{field-4}}\,\cdot \,{{field-5}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that multiplying the argument of a function by $k\ne 0$ represents the horizontal stretching of the corresponding graph by a factor of $\frac{1}{k}.$

Now, let $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x.$ Then, since $f(x)$ has a period of $2L,$ the function

$$
g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)
$$

must have a period of $2L\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}=2\pi .$ 

The Fourier series of $g(s)$ is

$$
g(s)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns),
$$

where:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x$ and using the fact that $g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s),$ we get the Fourier series of $f(x):$

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)
$$

Therefore, the constant term of $f(x)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $L=4$ and $f(x)={cos}^{2}⁡(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {\int }_{-4}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-35410282-5f4b-5357-9a5d-9ff9a6fd0203" "answer-field-20188161-12bf-54c3-b2b9-4680bbcd0ad2" $$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)

${a}_{4}=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the cosine coefficients are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{4} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{0}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(-2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{4}{[\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)]}_{-\pi }^{0}-\frac{2}{\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{4}{[\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{4\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-4\pi ))-\frac{1}{2\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ce23bf5e-8b29-5cf7-9b38-cc60d7fad1c9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-ce23bf5e-8b29-5cf7-9b38-cc60d7fad1c9" :answer-field/id #uuid "ce23bf5e-8b29-5cf7-9b38-cc60d7fad1c9" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-186b12e8-0537-5623-ab6f-d5dfb2e0cdcc" :answer-field/choices ["answer-186b12e8-0537-5623-ab6f-d5dfb2e0cdcc"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-186b12e8-0537-5623-ab6f-d5dfb2e0cdcc" :answer/id #uuid "186b12e8-0537-5623-ab6f-d5dfb2e0cdcc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186222514 :tutorial/content "When a function has period $2L$ (instead of $2\pi$), the "usual" Fourier formulas still work, but the sine and cosine inputs must be rescaled so that each term completes an integer number of oscillations over one period. 

We do this by converting the $2L$-periodic function into a $2\pi$-periodic one using a change of variables.

Let $f(x)$ be the $2L$-periodic extension of a function $F(x)$ from $x\in[-L,L)$ to $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
To use the standard $2\pi$-period Fourier formulas, define

$$
s=\frac{\pi}{L}x
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
g(s)=f\!\left(\frac{L}{\pi}s\right).
$$

Then $g$ is $2\pi$-periodic.

For a $2\pi$-periodic function $g$, the Fourier series is

$$
g(s)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\bigl(a_n\cos(ns)+b_n\sin(ns)\bigr),
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,ds, \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,ds,\,n\ge 1, \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,ds,\,n\ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute $g(s)=f\!\left(\dfrac{L}{\pi}s\right)$ and $s=\dfrac{\pi}{L}x$.
First, for $a_n{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,ds \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\,(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,ds \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f\,(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)cos\,(n\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,d\,(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)cos\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)cos\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Coefficients $b_n$ (for $n \geq 1$) and $a_0$ can be found similarly.

To summarize, the Fourier series of $f$ is

$$
f(x)\sim \frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(a_n\cos\!\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right)+b_n\sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right)\right),
$$

where the coefficients are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\,dx \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)cos\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)sin\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡({{field-1}})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡({{field-2}}).
$$

The $6$th sine coefficient of the series is

$$
{b}_{6}={{field-3}}.
$$

Given that $F(x)={x}^{3}$ and $L=3,$ the $6$th sine coefficient becomes

$$
{b}_{6}={{field-4}}\,\cdot \,{{field-5}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that multiplying the argument of a function by $k\ne 0$ represents the horizontal stretching of the corresponding graph by a factor of $\frac{1}{k}.$

Now, let $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x.$ Then, since $f(x)$ has a period of $2L,$ the function

$$
g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)
$$

must have a period of $2L\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}=2\pi .$ 

The Fourier series of $g(s)$ is

$$
g(s)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns),
$$

where:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x$ and using the fact that $g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s),$ we get the Fourier series of $f(x):$

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)
$$

Therefore, $6$th sine coefficient of $f(x)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{6} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(6s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(6s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{6\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{6\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $L=3$ and $f(x)={x}^{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{6} & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-3}^{3}{x}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{6\pi }{3}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {\int }_{-3}^{3}{x}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ce23bf5e-8b29-5cf7-9b38-cc60d7fad1c9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-ce23bf5e-8b29-5cf7-9b38-cc60d7fad1c9" :answer-field/id #uuid "ce23bf5e-8b29-5cf7-9b38-cc60d7fad1c9" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-186b12e8-0537-5623-ab6f-d5dfb2e0cdcc" :answer-field/choices ["answer-186b12e8-0537-5623-ab6f-d5dfb2e0cdcc"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-186b12e8-0537-5623-ab6f-d5dfb2e0cdcc" :answer/id #uuid "186b12e8-0537-5623-ab6f-d5dfb2e0cdcc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186222514 :tutorial/content "When a function has period $2L$ (instead of $2\pi$), the "usual" Fourier formulas still work, but the sine and cosine inputs must be rescaled so that each term completes an integer number of oscillations over one period. 

We do this by converting the $2L$-periodic function into a $2\pi$-periodic one using a change of variables.

Let $f(x)$ be the $2L$-periodic extension of a function $F(x)$ from $x\in[-L,L)$ to $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
To use the standard $2\pi$-period Fourier formulas, define

$$
s=\frac{\pi}{L}x
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
g(s)=f\!\left(\frac{L}{\pi}s\right).
$$

Then $g$ is $2\pi$-periodic.

For a $2\pi$-periodic function $g$, the Fourier series is

$$
g(s)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\bigl(a_n\cos(ns)+b_n\sin(ns)\bigr),
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,ds, \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,ds,\,n\ge 1, \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,ds,\,n\ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute $g(s)=f\!\left(\dfrac{L}{\pi}s\right)$ and $s=\dfrac{\pi}{L}x$.
First, for $a_n{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,ds \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\,(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,ds \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f\,(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)cos\,(n\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,d\,(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)cos\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)cos\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Coefficients $b_n$ (for $n \geq 1$) and $a_0$ can be found similarly.

To summarize, the Fourier series of $f$ is

$$
f(x)\sim \frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(a_n\cos\!\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right)+b_n\sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right)\right),
$$

where the coefficients are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\,dx \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)cos\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)sin\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem "Let $f(x)$ be the $2L$-periodic extension of a function $F(x)$ from $x\in [-L,L)$ to $x\in R.$
Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡({{field-1}})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡({{field-2}}).
$$

The $6$th sine coefficient of the series is

$$
{b}_{6}={{field-3}}.
$$

Given that $F(x)={x}^{3}$ and $L=3,$ the $6$th sine coefficient becomes

$$
{b}_{6}={{field-4}}\,\cdot \,{{field-5}}.
$$"] ["question-4886c497-1cb0-54c5-b33a-8a4433090897" :question/worked-solution "Recall that multiplying the argument of a function by $k\ne 0$ represents the horizontal stretching of the corresponding graph by a factor of $\frac{1}{k}.$

Now, let $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x.$ Then, since $f(x)$ has a period of $2L,$ the function

$$
g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)
$$

must have a period of $2L\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}=2\pi .$ 

The Fourier series of $g(s)$ is

$$
g(s)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns),
$$

where:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x$ and using the fact that $g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s),$ we get the Fourier series of $f(x):$

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)
$$

Therefore, $6$th sine coefficient of $f(x)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{6} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(6s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(6s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{6\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{6\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $L=3$ and $f(x)={x}^{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{6} & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-3}^{3}{x}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{6\pi }{3}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {\int }_{-3}^{3}{x}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-4886c497-1cb0-54c5-b33a-8a4433090897" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-a9d7c2b1-ebdc-5647-8fd1-cdc837ba2e78" :answer-field/id #uuid Now, let $s=\dfrac{\pi}{L}x.$ Then, since $f(x)$ has a period of $2L,$ the function

$$
g(s) = f\left(\dfrac{L}{\pi}s\right)
$$

must have a period of $2L \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{L} = 2\pi.$ 

The Fourier series of $g(s)$ is

$$
g(s) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n\cos(ns)+b_n\sin(ns),
$$

where:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $s=\dfrac{\pi}{L}x$ and using the fact that $g(s) = f\left(\dfrac{L}{\pi}s\right),$ we get the Fourier series of $f(x){:}$

$$
f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
a_n\cos\bigg(\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x}\bigg)+
b_n\sin\bigg(\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x}\bigg)
$$

Therefore, $4$th cosine coefficient of $f(x)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{4} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, $4$th sine coefficient of $f(x)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{4} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

We do this by converting the $2L$-periodic function into a $2\pi$-periodic one using a change of variables.

Let $f(x)$ be the $2L$-periodic extension of a function $F(x)$ from $x\in[-L,L)$ to $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
To use the standard $2\pi$-period Fourier formulas, define

$$
s=\frac{\pi}{L}x
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
g(s)=f\!\left(\frac{L}{\pi}s\right).
$$

Then $g$ is $2\pi$-periodic.

For a $2\pi$-periodic function $g$, the Fourier series is

$$
g(s)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\bigl(a_n\cos(ns)+b_n\sin(ns)\bigr),
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,ds, \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}(ns)\,ds,\,n\ge 1, \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}(ns)\,ds,\,n\ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute $g(s)=f\!\left(\dfrac{L}{\pi}s\right)$ and $s=\dfrac{\pi}{L}x$.
First, for $a_n{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}(ns)\,ds \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\,(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{cos}(ns)\,ds \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f\,(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)cos\,(n\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,d\,(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)cos\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)cos\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Coefficients $b_n$ (for $n \geq 1$) and $a_0$ can be found similarly.

To summarize, the Fourier series of $f$ is

$$
f(x)\sim \frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(a_n\cos\!\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right)+b_n\sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right)\right),
$$

where the coefficients are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\,dx \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)cos\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)sin\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$
